narrative:
The model predicts you have a 47% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The prediction is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed one class in the past. While students who passed had zero previous failures on average, your history of one failure strongly pushed the model toward expecting you to fail again. This single piece of information had the biggest influence on the outcome.

Two other factors worked in your favor but were not strong enough to overcome the past failure. First, your family has three or fewer members, which is less common among students who passed (only 34.5% of passers came from families this small). This smaller family size slightly reduced the predicted risk. Second, you spend 2 to 5 hours studying each week, which is the most common study habit among students who passed. This also nudged the prediction slightly toward passing, yet it could not offset the impact of your earlier academic setback.

To improve, focus on preventing any further failures by seeking extra academic support early, creating a more consistent study routine beyond your current 2–5 hours, and talking with your family or guardian about how they can help you stay on track. Addressing these areas now can still change your trajectory before the final exams.
